source_text: Τὸ μὲν οὖν ἄθεοι μὴ εἶναι, ἕνα τὸν ἀγένητον καὶ ἀΐδιον καὶ ἀόρατον καὶ ἀπαθῆ καὶ ἀκατάληπτον καὶ ἀχώρητον, νῷ μόνῳ καὶ λόγῳ καταλαμβανόμενον, φωτὶ καὶ κάλλει καὶ πνεύματι καὶ δυνάμει ἀνεκδιηγήτῳ περιεχόμενον, ὑφ᾿ οὗ γεγένηται τὸ πᾶν διὰ τοῦ αὐτοῦ λόγου καὶ διακεκόσμηται καὶ συγκρατεῖται, θεὸν ἄγοντες, ἱκανῶς μοι δέδεικται. Νοοῦμεν γὰρ καὶ υἱὸν τοῦ θεοῦ. Καὶ μή μοι γελοῖόν τις νομίσῃ τὸ υἱὸν εἶναι τῷ θεῷ. Οὐ γὰρ ὡς ποιηταὶ μυθοποιοῦσιν, οὐδὲν βελτίους τῶν ἀνθρώπων δεικνῦντες τοὺς θεούς, ἢ περὶ τοῦ θεοῦ καὶ πατρὸς ἢ περὶ τοῦ υἱοῦ πεφρονήκαμεν. Ἀλλ᾿ ἔστιν ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ θεοῦ λόγος τοῦ πατρὸς ἐν ἰδέᾳ καὶ ἐνεργείᾳ· πρὸς αὐτοῦ γὰρ καὶ δι᾿ αὐτοῦ πάντα ἐγένετο, ἑνὸς ὄντος τοῦ πατρὸς καὶ τοῦ υἱοῦ. Ὄντος δὲ τοῦ υἱοῦ ἐν πατρὶ καὶ πατρὸς ἐν υἱῷ, ἑνότητι καὶ δυνάμει πνεύματος, νοῦς καὶ λόγος τοῦ πατρὸς ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ θεοῦ. Εἰ δὲ δι᾿ ὑπερβολὴν συνέσεως σκοπεῖν ὑμῖν ἔπεισιν, ὁ παῖς τί βούλεται, ἐρῶ διὰ βραχέων πρῶτον γέννημα εἶναι τῷ πατρί, οὐχ ὡς γενόμενον (ἐξ ἀρχῆς γὰρ ὁ θεός, νοῦς ἀΐδιος ὤν, εἶχεν αὐτὸς ἐν ἑαυτῷ τὸν λόγον, ἀϊδίως λογικὸς ὤν), ἀλλ᾿ ὡς τῶν ὑλικῶν ξυμπάντων, ἀποίου φύσεως καὶ γῆς ἀχρείας ὑποκειμένων δίκην, μεμιγμένων τῶν παχυμερεστέρων πρὸς τὰ κουφότερα ἐπ᾿ αὐτοῖς, ἰδέα καὶ ἐνέργεια εἶναι προελθών. Συνᾴδει δὲ τῷ λόγῳ καὶ τὸ προφητικὸν πνεῦμα· Κύριος γάρ, φησίν, ἔκτισέ με ἀρχὴν ὁδῶν αὐτοῦ εἰς ἔργα αὐτοῦ. Καίτοι καὶ αὐτὸ τὸ ἐνεργοῦν τοῖς ἐκφωνοῦσι προφητικῶς ἅγιον πνεῦμα ἀπόῤῥοιαν εἶναί φαμεν τοῦ θεοῦ, ἀποῤῥέον καὶ ἐπαναφερόμενον ὡς ἀκτῖνα ἡλίου.Τίς οὖν οὐκ ἂν ἀπορήσαι, λέγοντας θεὸν πατέρα καὶ υἱὸν θεὸν καὶ πνεῦμα ἅγιον, δεικνύντας αὐτῶν καὶ τὴν ἐν τῇ ἑνώσει δύναμιν καὶ τὴν ἐν τῇ τάξει διαίρεσιν, ἀκούσας ἀθέους καλουμένους; Καὶ οὐκ ἐπὶ τούτοις τὸ θεολογικὸν ἡμῶν ἵσταται μέρος· ἀλλὰ καὶ πλῆθος ἀγγέλων καὶ λειτουργῶν φαμεν, οὓς ὁ ποιητὴς καὶ δημιουργὸς κόσμου θεὸς διὰ τοῦ παρ᾿ αὐτοῦ λόγου διένειμε καὶ διέταξε περί τε τὰ στοιχεῖα εἶναι καὶ τοὺς οὐρανοὺς καὶ τὸν κόσμον καὶ τὰ ἐν αὐτῷ καὶ τὴν τούτων εὐταξίαν.
pass_a_gloss: That therefore we are not atheists, one unborn and eternal and invisible and impassive and incomprehensible and uncircumscribed, being apprehended by mind alone and reason, being encompassed by light and beauty and spirit and indescribable power, by whom all things have been made through his own reason and have been adorned and are held together, having been shown to me sufficiently. For we think also of the Son of God. And let no one think it laughable that the Son is of God. For not as poets mythologize, showing the gods to be no better than men, nor have we thought about God and Father or about the Son. But the Son of God is the reason of the Father in idea and in energy; for through him and on account of him all things have been made, the Father and the Son being one. And the Son being in the Father and the Father in the Son, by unity and power of spirit, the Son of God is the mind and reason of the Father. And if it persuades you to consider by excess of understanding, what the child wants, I will say briefly that he is the firstborn of the Father, not as having been made (for God was from the beginning, being an eternal mind, having the reason in himself eternally, being eternally rational), but as the idea and energy have proceeded, the material things all having been subjected, of a useless nature and useless earth, the thicker things having been mixed with the lighter things upon them. And the prophetic spirit agrees with the reason; for it says, The Lord made me the beginning of his ways for his works. And we say that the holy spirit which energizes in those who speak prophetically is an effluence of God, flowing out and being reflected back like a ray of the sun. Who then would not be at a loss, speaking of God the Father and Son of God and Holy Spirit, showing both their power in unity and their distinction in order, having been called atheists? And our theological part does not stand on these things; but we also say a multitude of angels and ministers, whom the maker and creator of the world God has distributed and ordered through his reason which is with him, concerning both the elements and the heavens and the world and the things in it and their good order.

choices.why: refers to those who do not believe in God
refers to Jesus Christ as the son of God
refers to the third person of the Trinity

bible_refs.note: The Lord made me the beginning of his ways for his works

pass_b_english: That we are not atheists has been shown to me sufficiently, for we hold to one God, unborn, eternal, invisible, impassible, incomprehensible, and uncircumscribed, who is apprehended by mind and reason alone and encompassed by light, beauty, spirit, and indescribable power. Through his own Reason all things have been made, adorned, and are held together. We also acknowledge the Son of God. Let no one think it laughable that the Son belongs to God. We have not thought of God and Father, nor of the Son, as poets mythologize, making the gods no better than men. Rather, the Son of God is the Reason of the Father in idea and in energy; for through him and on account of him all things were made, the Father and the Son being one. Since the Son is in the Father and the Father in the Son, by unity and power of Spirit, the Son of God is the mind and Reason of the Father. If you are persuaded to consider this by excess of understanding, I will say briefly what the Child desires: he is the firstborn of the Father, not as having been made (for God was from the beginning, an eternal mind, having the Reason in himself eternally, being eternally rational), but as idea and energy proceeding, all material things having been subjected — of useless nature and useless earth — the denser things mixed with the lighter upon them. The prophetic Spirit agrees with the Reason; for it says, "The Lord created me the beginning of his ways for his works" (Proverbs 8:22). We also say that the Holy Spirit which energizes those who speak prophetically is an effluence of God, flowing out and reflected back like a ray of the sun.

Who then would not be at a loss, hearing us called atheists while we speak of God the Father, the Son of God, and the Holy Spirit, showing both their power in unity and their distinction in order? Our theological account does not rest on these things alone; we also affirm a multitude of angels and ministers, whom the Maker and Creator of the world, God, has distributed and ordered through his Reason which is with him, to govern the elements, the heavens, the world, the things in it, and their good order.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the complex theological distinctions of the Greek text, including the attributes of God, the relationship between Father and Son, and the nature of the Holy Spirit. Pass B correctly identifies the scripture allusion (Proverbs 8:22) which was only implied in the Greek. Pass A and B are consistent with the Greek source.
